performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra, Stanisław Wisłocki
intro: Sviatoslav Richter begins with the piano’s tolling chords, then pours out arpeggios beneath the orchestra’s first melody. Rachmaninoff’s Second Concerto makes its soloist an accompanist before letting him sing.

sections.label: Intro · Piano bells over low F
sections.mNote: Repeated chords grow from pp above a recurring bass note

sections.label: A · Strings sing in C minor
sections.mNote: The piano’s arpeggios accompany strings and clarinet

sections.label: B · The piano sings in E♭
sections.mNote: A long melody replaces the soloist’s running accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · Themes pass between piano and winds
sections.mNote: Short phrases travel through changing keys

sections.label: A′ · The tune returns against a march
sections.mNote: The orchestra sings while the piano presses forward in chords

sections.label: B′ · A solo horn in A♭
sections.mNote: The second tune returns over quiet string chords

sections.mNote: The first theme returns softly before the final acceleration

relations.label: The first-subject music returns
relations.basis: The first subject and its associated material return in the recapitulation with changed piano writing. The excerpts lie in the later part of the opening subject group and its returning continuation, rather than at the large climax itself. CENS diagonal mean 0.931, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 369.5 s (cache/form/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-moderato.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: The piano becomes a bell
cues.text: The orchestra waits. The piano strikes a chord, reaches down to a low F and begins again. Each toll grows stronger, from pp towards f; only after this slow gathering does the first tune arrive.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, p. 3: solo piano introduction, recurring low F and poco a poco crescendo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune over restless hands
cues.text: Violins, violas and clarinet sing the C minor melody. Beneath them, the piano sweeps up and down in broken chords, while cellos and double basses pluck the bass notes. The soloist has the busiest part and somebody else has the tune.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 3–4, rehearsal 1: C minor first subject, piano arpeggios and pizzicato lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dahl’s daily promise
cues.text: “You will begin to write your concerto.” In the first months of 1900, Dr Nikolai Dahl repeats that promise to Rachmaninoff during their daily treatment sessions. After the failure of his First Symphony, the composer is struggling to write. The new concerto will carry Dahl’s name on its dedication page.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note quotes Dahl’s words to Rachmaninoff, dates the daily sessions January–April 1900 and documents the dedication. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: The soloist gets the song
cues.text: The piano takes the long second melody in E♭ major. Its upper notes sing over its own broken chords; the orchestra leaves space around them. The instrument that carried the first tune’s accompaniment now carries both parts.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement’s second subject and continuation, pp. 12–15; the E♭ major piano theme is also described in the work’s structural overview. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tunes break into phrases
cues.text: The long melodies break into shorter phrases. Piano and woodwinds pass them back and forth, changing keys as they go. A march-like rhythm begins to take shape in the piano; it will stand against the returning first tune.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement development; the emerging march-like idea and its later combination with the first subject are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Moscow, November 1901
cues.text: On 9 November 1901 Rachmaninoff sits at the piano in Moscow for the first complete performance. His cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti conducts. The Adagio and finale already have a successful première behind them; the first movement is the new arrival.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note gives the complete première, Siloti’s relationship to Rachmaninoff and the earlier performance of the last two movements. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: A march beneath the melody
cues.text: The orchestra brings back the first tune in C minor. The piano answers with hard, marching chords in place of its original arpeggios. Two ideas fill the same space: the broad melody above and the insistent rhythm below.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement recapitulation; the march-like piano counterline against the returning first subject is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A horn left singing
cues.text: A solo horn takes the second melody in A♭ major, marked p dolce. The piano falls silent. Quiet repeated string chords leave the horn’s long notes exposed after the crowded march.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 40, rehearsal 13: solo horn, p dolce, A♭ major and repeated pp string chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet start to the coda
cues.text: Meno mosso: the first tune returns softly in the strings, over small piano figures. Rachmaninoff holds the ending back before the final acceleration. The movement closes in C minor; the concerto still has two movements to reach C major.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 44–47, rehearsal 16 and conclusion: Meno mosso, pp strings and piano, then the C minor close; the finale ends in C major.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bells turn into arpeggios
transitions.from: Intro · Piano bells over low F
transitions.to: A · Strings sing in C minor
transitions.how: The repeated low F makes way for C, and the piano opens its solid chords into arpeggios. Violins, violas and clarinet begin the C minor theme, marked con passione in the strings. Cellos and double basses pluck the bass beneath the soloist’s moving hands.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, pp. 3–4, rehearsal 1.

transitions.title: The piano takes the melody
transitions.from: A · Strings sing in C minor
transitions.to: B · The piano sings in E♭
transitions.how: The quick più mosso piano passage drives through cadences towards E♭ major. The sound then softens and the piano begins the second melody, sustained above its own broken chords. Short woodwind answers surround the solo line.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement transition and E♭ major second subject; structural account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: The long tunes become short exchanges
transitions.from: B · The piano sings in E♭
transitions.to: Dev · Themes pass between piano and winds
transitions.how: The E♭ major closing rush subsides. Woodwind phrases and piano figures take up fragments of the two themes, repeating them over changing bass notes. The melody moves from one instrument to another as the harmony leaves the exposition’s settled keys.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement development; its use of both themes and changing orchestration is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: The orchestra sings over the march
transitions.from: Dev · Themes pass between piano and winds
transitions.to: A′ · The tune returns against a march
transitions.how: The accelerating piano chords and brass calls lead straight into the C minor return. The orchestra restores the first melody while the piano keeps the march-like rhythm developed in the middle. The home tune arrives in the thick of the crescendo.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement development and recapitulation; the combination of first theme and march-like piano writing is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: A quiet chord leaves the horn
transitions.from: A′ · The tune returns against a march
transitions.to: B′ · A solo horn in A♭
transitions.how: The piano descends chromatically and settles on an A♭ major chord at ppp. It then rests while a solo horn sings the second subject, p dolce. The strings repeat soft chords underneath; the tune that belonged to the piano now fits inside a single horn phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 39–40, rehearsal 13: descending piano line, A♭ major chord and solo horn.

transitions.title: The first tune returns softly
transitions.from: B′ · A solo horn in A♭
transitions.to: Coda · Meno mosso, then C minor
transitions.how: The late piano arpeggios touch C major before the coda turns back towards C minor. At Meno mosso, the strings recall the first tune at pp, with short piano figures above a slower-moving bass. The final drive grows out of this quiet return.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 44–47, rehearsal 16 and conclusion; the preceding C major arpeggios and C minor coda are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

source.title: Rachmaninoff, Piano Concerto No. 2, I. Moderato, full score (Gutheil; Boosey & Hawkes reprint)
source.locator: Printed pp. 3–47, rehearsal figures 1–16: piano introduction, orchestral first theme, E♭ major piano melody, march-like return and A♭ major horn solo.

timeline.note: The piano’s repeated chords grow stronger over a recurring low F.
Clarinet and upper strings sing the C minor tune; cellos and basses pluck beneath the piano arpeggios.
The string melody broadens, with wind and horn chords around the piano’s running notes.
Piano figures pass between held flute and clarinet chords and short horn and string answers.
The piano sings the E♭ major second tune, with quiet strings and short woodwind replies.
Woodwinds answer the piano; brass and timpani strengthen the exposition’s closing phrases.
Piano and woodwinds exchange fragments of the themes over held and repeated string chords.
Flutes and oboes sing long notes against the piano’s quicker figures, supported by horns and lower strings.
Brass calls rise above the piano’s chordal rhythm as the strings join the crescendo.
The orchestra brings back the first tune in C minor against the piano’s marching chords.
The piano continues the tune as the brass falls silent and woodwinds answer over quieter strings.
A solo horn sings the second tune in A♭ major, with repeated string chords and the piano at rest.
The piano’s late arpeggios run between soft wind chords and sustained string lines.
Unmuted strings recall the first tune at Meno mosso, with quiet piano figures, bassoon and horn.
Winds, brass and timpani join piano and strings for the final C minor chords.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
